title: Population Genetics II — Inheritance, Hardy–Weinberg & Diversity

cards.explanation: The lecture extends inheritance in individual families to population-level allele and genotype frequencies.
cards.text: Population genetics studies genetic variation in populations and how it {{c1::changes over time}}.
cards.question: Population genetics studies genetic variation in populations and how it {{c1::changes over time}}.

cards.explanation: It follows one maternal lineage, not all of a person’s ancestors or their complete genome-wide ancestry.
cards.text: Mitochondrial DNA primarily traces {{c1::matrilineal ancestry}}.
cards.question: Mitochondrial DNA primarily traces {{c1::matrilineal ancestry}}.

cards.explanation: This concerns a paternal lineage in people carrying that chromosome, not a complete account of ancestry.
cards.text: The non-recombining portion of the Y chromosome traces {{c1::patrilineal ancestry}}.
cards.question: The non-recombining portion of the Y chromosome traces {{c1::patrilineal ancestry}}.

cards.explanation: The diagram distinguishes an allele from the pair of alleles making up a diploid genotype.
cards.text: An alternative version of a gene at a locus is an {{c1::allele}}.
cards.question: An alternative version of a gene at a locus is an {{c1::allele}}.

cards.explanation: The figure shows PP, Pp and pp as different genotypes.
cards.text: The pair of alleles at a diploid locus is the {{c1::genotype}}.
cards.question: The pair of alleles at a diploid locus is the {{c1::genotype}}.

cards.explanation: Different genotypes can share a phenotype under complete dominance, as PP and Pp do in the figure.
cards.text: An observable trait, such as flower colour, is a {{c1::phenotype}}.
cards.question: An observable trait, such as flower colour, is a {{c1::phenotype}}.

cards.explanation: For the modelled autosomal locus, each gamete receives one of the two alleles.
cards.text: The separation of a diploid individual’s two alleles during meiosis is the law of {{c1::segregation}}.
cards.question: The separation of a diploid individual’s two alleles during meiosis is the law of {{c1::segregation}}.

cards.explanation: Qualification to the slide: physically linked loci may be inherited together, so independence is not a universal rule for every gene pair.
cards.text: Independent assortment applies to loci that are {{c1::unlinked or effectively unlinked}}.
cards.question: Independent assortment applies to loci that are {{c1::unlinked or effectively unlinked}}.

cards.explanation: The slide’s statement that recessive expression is “always” masked applies to its complete-dominance model, not codominance or incomplete dominance.
cards.text: Under complete dominance, a heterozygote shows the {{c1::dominant phenotype}}.
cards.question: Under complete dominance, a heterozygote shows the {{c1::dominant phenotype}}.

cards.explanation: Dominance describes heterozygote expression, not allele frequency, fitness or an automatic increase over generations.
cards.text: A dominant allele need not be {{c1::common}} in a population.
cards.question: A dominant allele need not be {{c1::common}} in a population.

cards.explanation: The homozygous parents contribute T and t respectively; the expected offspring are all heterozygotes.
cards.text: In the lecture’s TT × tt pea cross, every offspring has genotype {{c1::Tt}}.
cards.question: In the lecture’s TT × tt pea cross, every offspring has genotype {{c1::Tt}}.

cards.explanation: All offspring are Tt. The result is an expected phenotype distribution for the stated model, not a general rule for all tall-by-short crosses.
cards.text: Under complete dominance, the TT × tt cross produces {{c1::100% tall}} offspring.
cards.question: Under complete dominance, the TT × tt cross produces {{c1::100% tall}} offspring.

cards.explanation: The four equally likely gamete combinations are TT, Tt, tT and tt; Tt and tT are the same heterozygous genotype.
cards.text: In a Tt × Tt cross, the expected TT:Tt:tt genotype ratio is {{c1::1:2:1}}.
cards.question: In a Tt × Tt cross, the expected TT:Tt:tt genotype ratio is {{c1::1:2:1}}.

cards.explanation: TT and Tt are tall; only tt is short. This is an expected probability ratio, not a promise about four actual offspring.
cards.text: With T completely dominant, a Tt × Tt cross has a tall:short phenotype ratio of {{c1::3:1}}.
cards.question: With T completely dominant, a Tt × Tt cross has a tall:short phenotype ratio of {{c1::3:1}}.

cards.explanation: Each parent transmits t with probability 1/2, so P(tt)=1/2 ×1/2.
cards.text: A short offspring from two heterozygous tall plants has probability {{c1::1/4}}.
cards.question: A short offspring from two heterozygous tall plants has probability {{c1::1/4}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture models wet W as completely dominant over dry w; a dry-phenotype parent contributes w.
cards.text: In the earwax example, dry earwax has genotype {{c1::ww}}.
cards.question: In the earwax example, dry earwax has genotype {{c1::ww}}.

cards.explanation: The Ww parent contributes w half the time; the ww parent always contributes w. The other half are Ww.
cards.text: For Ww × ww in the earwax model, the probability of a dry-earwax child is {{c1::50%}}.
cards.question: For Ww × ww in the earwax model, the probability of a dry-earwax child is {{c1::50%}}.

cards.explanation: The source example follows yellow/green colour and round/wrinkled shape in peas.
cards.text: A cross following two loci simultaneously is a {{c1::dihybrid cross}}.
cards.question: A cross following two loci simultaneously is a {{c1::dihybrid cross}}.

cards.explanation: This assumes normal segregation and no linkage affecting these loci.
cards.text: With independent assortment, YyRr produces YR, Yr, yR and yr gametes at {{c1::equal 1/4 probabilities}}.
cards.question: With independent assortment, YyRr produces YR, Yr, yR and yr gametes at {{c1::equal 1/4 probabilities}}.

cards.explanation: Multiply the 3/4 dominant and 1/4 recessive probabilities at each locus: 9/16,3/16,3/16,1/16. The phenotype labels fix the ratio’s order.
cards.text: For YyRr × YyRr with independent assortment and complete dominance, yellow-round:yellow-wrinkled:green-round:green-wrinkled is {{c1::9:3:3:1}}.
cards.question: For YyRr × YyRr with independent assortment and complete dominance, yellow-round:yellow-wrinkled:green-round:green-wrinkled is {{c1::9:3:3:1}}.

cards.explanation: P(yy)=1/4 and P(rr)=1/4; independent events multiply.
cards.text: For independently assorting YyRr parents, P(yyrr) is {{c1::1/16}}.
cards.question: For independently assorting YyRr parents, P(yyrr) is {{c1::1/16}}.

cards.explanation: Mendelian segregation preserves alleles under the Hardy–Weinberg model. The red-hair example is simplified: actual human hair colour involves multiple variants and genes.
cards.text: A recessive allele does not automatically {{c1::disappear}} merely because it is masked in heterozygotes.
cards.question: A recessive allele does not automatically {{c1::disappear}} merely because it is masked in heterozygotes.

cards.explanation: p and q are proportions of allele copies, not the proportions of dominant and recessive phenotypes.
cards.text: For a two-allele locus, allele frequencies satisfy {{c1::p + q = 1}}.
cards.question: For a two-allele locus, allele frequencies satisfy {{c1::p + q = 1}}.

cards.text: If p=0.7 and q=0.3, the expected AA frequency is {{c1::0.49}}.
cards.question: If p=0.7 and q=0.3, the expected AA frequency is {{c1::0.49}}.

cards.explanation: 2pq=2×0.7×0.3; the two parental allele orderings must both be counted.
cards.text: If p=0.7 and q=0.3, the expected Aa frequency is {{c1::0.42}}.
cards.question: If p=0.7 and q=0.3, the expected Aa frequency is {{c1::0.42}}.

cards.explanation: q²=0.3×0.3; the three genotype frequencies are 0.49,0.42,0.09.
cards.text: If p=0.7 and q=0.3, the expected aa frequency is {{c1::0.09}}.
cards.question: If p=0.7 and q=0.3, the expected aa frequency is {{c1::0.09}}.

cards.explanation: p=f(AA)+½f(Aa)=0.49+0.21. Counting alleles this way does not itself require HWE.
cards.text: From genotype frequencies f(AA)=0.49 and f(Aa)=0.42, the A allele frequency is {{c1::0.70}}.
cards.question: From genotype frequencies f(AA)=0.49 and f(Aa)=0.42, the A allele frequency is {{c1::0.70}}.

cards.explanation: This follows from independent sampling of A with probability p from each parental gamete pool.
cards.text: At Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, the AA genotype frequency is {{c1::p²}}.
cards.question: At Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, the AA genotype frequency is {{c1::p²}}.

cards.explanation: Either A-then-a or a-then-A produces the same Aa genotype, giving pq+pq.
cards.text: At Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, the heterozygote frequency is {{c1::2pq}}.
cards.question: At Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, the heterozygote frequency is {{c1::2pq}}.

cards.explanation: Do not confuse the recessive genotype frequency q² with the recessive allele frequency q.
cards.text: At Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, the aa genotype frequency is {{c1::q²}}.
cards.question: At Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, the aa genotype frequency is {{c1::q²}}.

cards.explanation: The three mutually exclusive diploid genotypes account for the whole modelled population.
cards.text: The two-allele Hardy–Weinberg genotype frequencies sum as {{c1::p² + 2pq + q² = 1}}.
cards.question: The two-allele Hardy–Weinberg genotype frequencies sum as {{c1::p² + 2pq + q² = 1}}.

cards.explanation: Random mating and Mendelian segregation alone do not force dominant alleles to replace recessive ones.
cards.text: Under the ideal model, allele frequencies remain {{c1::constant across generations}}.
cards.question: Under the ideal model, allele frequencies remain {{c1::constant across generations}}.

cards.explanation: Allele frequencies can be preserved while genotype proportions reach the random-mating distribution; allele stability and genotype proportions are distinct ideas.
cards.text: For a randomly mating population with the model assumptions, genotype proportions follow {{c1::p²:2pq:q²}}.
cards.question: For a randomly mating population with the model assumptions, genotype proportions follow {{c1::p²:2pq:q²}}.

cards.explanation: It changes genotype proportions, commonly increasing homozygosity, without necessarily changing allele frequencies by itself.
cards.text: Mating between close relatives is {{c1::inbreeding}}.
cards.question: Mating between close relatives is {{c1::inbreeding}}.

cards.explanation: The slide uses “assortative” for similarity. Effects depend on the trait and loci involved, rather than every locus changing identically.
cards.text: Choosing mates with similar characteristics is {{c1::positive assortative mating}}.
cards.question: Choosing mates with similar characteristics is {{c1::positive assortative mating}}.

cards.explanation: This distinction prevents treating every departure from HWE proportions as evidence of a changed allele pool.
cards.text: Non-random mating can change genotype frequencies without directly changing {{c1::allele frequencies}}.
cards.question: Non-random mating can change genotype frequencies without directly changing {{c1::allele frequencies}}.

cards.explanation: Gene flow can change local allele frequencies if the source and receiving populations differ.
cards.text: Migration followed by interbreeding between populations can produce {{c1::admixture}}.
cards.question: Migration followed by interbreeding between populations can produce {{c1::admixture}}.

cards.explanation: Recombination usually reshuffles existing variants rather than creating a new allele at the locus.
cards.text: The process introducing a new DNA sequence variant is {{c1::mutation}}.
cards.question: The process introducing a new DNA sequence variant is {{c1::mutation}}.

cards.explanation: It can change associations between loci without directly changing a single-locus allele frequency. The source groups mutation and recombination together, but their effects differ.
cards.text: Recombination changes combinations of alleles into new {{c1::haplotypes}}.
cards.question: Recombination changes combinations of alleles into new {{c1::haplotypes}}.

cards.explanation: Different environments can favour different variants; fitness concerns reproductive contribution, not simply physical strength.
cards.text: Differential survival and reproduction associated with heritable variation is {{c1::natural selection}}.
cards.question: Differential survival and reproduction associated with heritable variation is {{c1::natural selection}}.

cards.explanation: The surviving allele pool may be an unrepresentative sample of the original population.
cards.text: A sudden reduction in the number of reproducing individuals is a population {{c1::bottleneck}}.
cards.question: A sudden reduction in the number of reproducing individuals is a population {{c1::bottleneck}}.

cards.explanation: Population numbers may later recover without restoring lost variants immediately.
cards.text: A bottleneck can reduce genetic variation by {{c1::chance loss of alleles}}.
cards.question: A bottleneck can reduce genetic variation by {{c1::chance loss of alleles}}.

cards.explanation: Unlike selection, the change need not reflect a fitness advantage.
cards.text: Random changes in allele frequency caused by sampling across generations are {{c1::genetic drift}}.
cards.question: Random changes in allele frequency caused by sampling across generations are {{c1::genetic drift}}.

cards.explanation: Sampling fluctuations have greater relative effects when fewer individuals contribute to reproduction.
cards.text: Genetic drift is generally stronger in {{c1::small populations}}.
cards.question: Genetic drift is generally stronger in {{c1::small populations}}.

cards.explanation: Allele a has been lost in this illustration; fixation does not by itself demonstrate a selective advantage.
cards.text: In the rabbit diagram, p=1 and q=0 in the final generation represent A allele {{c1::fixation}}.
cards.question: In the rabbit diagram, p=1 and q=0 in the final generation represent A allele {{c1::fixation}}.

cards.explanation: This is the count underlying 2N allele copies in N diploid individuals.
cards.text: The lecture’s diploid model assigns {{c1::two allele copies per autosomal locus}} to each individual.
cards.question: The lecture’s diploid model assigns {{c1::two allele copies per autosomal locus}} to each individual.
cards.answer: two allele copies per autosomal locus

cards.explanation: This is the setting for the Punnett-square probability argument.
cards.text: The introductory derivation assumes {{c1::sexual reproduction}} with gametes combining.
cards.question: The introductory derivation assumes {{c1::sexual reproduction}} with gametes combining.

cards.explanation: This simplifies the model; it does not mean overlapping human generations make all HWE calculations useless.
cards.text: The lecture’s generation-by-generation model assumes {{c1::non-overlapping generations}}.
cards.question: The lecture’s generation-by-generation model assumes {{c1::non-overlapping generations}}.

cards.explanation: Hardy–Weinberg principles can be generalised to more alleles; two alleles are a limit of this algebraic form, not of the whole principle.
cards.text: Using just p and q assumes the modelled locus has {{c1::two alleles}}.
cards.question: Using just p and q assumes the modelled locus has {{c1::two alleles}}.

cards.explanation: This permits the same p and q to be used on both axes of the square.
cards.text: The lecture assumes equal allele frequencies in the {{c1::male and female gamete pools}}.
cards.question: The lecture assumes equal allele frequencies in the {{c1::male and female gamete pools}}.

cards.explanation: Without genotype-associated fitness differences, selection does not shift the allele pool.
cards.text: Equal survival and reproductive success among genotypes represents {{c1::no selection}}.
cards.question: Equal survival and reproductive success among genotypes represents {{c1::no selection}}.

cards.explanation: This is distinct from the no-migration assumption.
cards.text: The assumption preventing generation of new alleles during the model is {{c1::no mutation}}.
cards.question: The assumption preventing generation of new alleles during the model is {{c1::no mutation}}.

cards.explanation: Migration can matter when the incoming or outgoing allele frequencies differ.
cards.text: The assumption excluding gene flow into or out of the population is {{c1::no migration}}.
cards.question: The assumption excluding gene flow into or out of the population is {{c1::no migration}}.

cards.explanation: Real populations are finite; the approximation can be useful when sampling effects are small.
cards.text: An infinitely large population is assumed to remove {{c1::genetic drift}}.
cards.question: An infinitely large population is assumed to remove {{c1::genetic drift}}.

cards.explanation: For a locus-level application, randomness concerns the genotype at the locus being studied, not every possible social or behavioural trait.
cards.text: The mating assumption in the Hardy–Weinberg model is {{c1::random mating}}.
cards.question: The mating assumption in the Hardy–Weinberg model is {{c1::random mating}}.

cards.explanation: Compare observed data with a baseline before investigating departures. Real populations need not perfectly satisfy every introductory assumption to make this comparison useful.
cards.text: Hardy–Weinberg is useful as a {{c1::null model}} for expected genotype proportions.
cards.question: Hardy–Weinberg is useful as a {{c1::null model}} for expected genotype proportions.

cards.explanation: It is written Δ32. CCR5 participates in HIV entry; the example connects genotype with a medically relevant phenotype.
cards.text: The CCR5 variant in the lecture has a {{c1::32-base-pair deletion}}.
cards.question: The CCR5 variant in the lecture has a {{c1::32-base-pair deletion}}.

cards.explanation: The slide’s unqualified “HIV-1 resistant” label is simplified: this is not universal immunity against every HIV strain or a reason to disregard prevention.
cards.text: CCR5 Δ32 homozygosity strongly reduces susceptibility to {{c1::CCR5-tropic HIV-1}}.
cards.question: CCR5 Δ32 homozygosity strongly reduces susceptibility to {{c1::CCR5-tropic HIV-1}}.

cards.explanation: This is an association in the teaching example, not a guarantee of an individual clinical course.
cards.text: In the lecture model, a normal/Δ32 heterozygote is associated with {{c1::slower progression to AIDS}}.
cards.question: In the lecture model, a normal/Δ32 heterozygote is associated with {{c1::slower progression to AIDS}}.

cards.explanation: Each individual contributes two allele copies, regardless of whether homozygous or heterozygous.
cards.text: For 100 diploid individuals at one autosomal locus, the allele-copy denominator is {{c1::200}}.
cards.question: For 100 diploid individuals at one autosomal locus, the allele-copy denominator is {{c1::200}}.

cards.explanation: Two copies from the variant homozygote plus one from each heterozygote: 2×1+20.
cards.text: With 79 normal homozygotes, 20 heterozygotes and 1 Δ32 homozygote, the Δ32 allele count is {{c1::22}}.
cards.question: With 79 normal homozygotes, 20 heterozygotes and 1 Δ32 homozygote, the Δ32 allele count is {{c1::22}}.

cards.explanation: q=22/200=11%; the frequency of Δ32 homozygotes is a different quantity.
cards.text: For the sample with 22 Δ32 copies among 200 alleles, q is {{c1::0.11}}.
cards.question: For the sample with 22 Δ32 copies among 200 alleles, q is {{c1::0.11}}.

cards.explanation: p=1−q. Direct counting also gives (2×79+20)/200.
cards.text: If the Δ32 allele frequency is q=0.11, the normal allele frequency p is {{c1::0.89}}.
cards.question: If the Δ32 allele frequency is q=0.11, the normal allele frequency p is {{c1::0.89}}.

cards.explanation: q²=0.11²=1.21%, corresponding to 1.21 expected individuals in a sample of 100, not a guaranteed exact count.
cards.text: With q=0.11, the HWE expected Δ32/Δ32 proportion is {{c1::0.0121}}.
cards.question: With q=0.11, the HWE expected Δ32/Δ32 proportion is {{c1::0.0121}}.

cards.explanation: 2pq=2×0.89×0.11=19.58%. Observed heterozygosity in the sample is 20%.
cards.text: With p=0.89 and q=0.11, expected heterozygosity is {{c1::0.1958}}.
cards.question: With p=0.89 and q=0.11, expected heterozygosity is {{c1::0.1958}}.

cards.explanation: Expected counts are 79.21,19.58,1.21. The slide declares equilibrium, but visual closeness alone is not a formal statistical test or proof that no evolutionary forces act.
cards.text: The observed 79:20:1 CCR5 counts are {{c1::close to the HWE expectation}}.
cards.question: The observed 79:20:1 CCR5 counts are {{c1::close to the HWE expectation}}.

cards.explanation: p=(2×5+70)/(2×100)=80/200. Allele counting remains valid even if genotype proportions depart from HWE.
cards.text: For counts 5 a¹a¹, 70 a¹a² and 25 a²a², the a¹ allele frequency is {{c1::0.40}}.
cards.question: For counts 5 a¹a¹, 70 a¹a² and 25 a²a², the a¹ allele frequency is {{c1::0.40}}.

cards.text: If a¹ has frequency 0.40 in the exercise, a² has frequency {{c1::0.60}}.
cards.question: If a¹ has frequency 0.40 in the exercise, a² has frequency {{c1::0.60}}.

cards.explanation: p²×100=0.16×100. The observed count is 5.
cards.text: For p=0.40 and q=0.60 in 100 people, the expected a¹a¹ count is {{c1::16}}.
cards.question: For p=0.40 and q=0.60 in 100 people, the expected a¹a¹ count is {{c1::16}}.

cards.explanation: 2pq×100=0.48×100. The observed count is 70.
cards.text: For p=0.40 and q=0.60 in 100 people, the expected heterozygote count is {{c1::48}}.
cards.question: For p=0.40 and q=0.60 in 100 people, the expected heterozygote count is {{c1::48}}.

cards.explanation: q²×100=0.36×100. The observed count is 25.
cards.text: For p=0.40 and q=0.60 in 100 people, the expected a²a² count is {{c1::36}}.
cards.question: For p=0.40 and q=0.60 in 100 people, the expected a²a² count is {{c1::36}}.

cards.explanation: Both homozygote classes are below expectation. The table alone does not identify a cause or justify attributing the difference to one specific force.
cards.text: Observed heterozygosity of 70% versus an HWE expectation of 48% is a {{c1::heterozygote excess}}.
cards.question: Observed heterozygosity of 70% versus an HWE expectation of 48% is a {{c1::heterozygote excess}}.

cards.explanation: This assumes the simplified two-allele HWE model and that the recessive genotype explains the stated frequency; it is not a current universal CF prevalence estimate.
cards.text: In the recessive CF exercise, disease frequency 1/2500 corresponds to {{c1::q²}}.
cards.question: In the recessive CF exercise, disease frequency 1/2500 corresponds to {{c1::q²}}.

cards.explanation: Take the square root: √0.0004=0.02. Do not use q² itself as q.
cards.text: If q²=1/2500=0.0004, the disease-allele frequency q is {{c1::0.02}}.
cards.question: If q²=1/2500=0.0004, the disease-allele frequency q is {{c1::0.02}}.

cards.explanation: p=1−0.02; p and q count alleles, not people with each phenotype.
cards.text: For the CF exercise with q=0.02, p is {{c1::0.98}}.
cards.question: For the CF exercise with q=0.02, p is {{c1::0.98}}.

cards.explanation: 2pq=2×0.98×0.02=0.0392, about 1 in 25.5 people. This gives a proportion; an absolute count requires a population size.
cards.text: For q=0.02 and p=0.98, the unaffected carrier frequency is {{c1::3.92%}}.
cards.question: For q=0.02 and p=0.98, the unaffected carrier frequency is {{c1::3.92%}}.

cards.explanation: Here 2q=4%, while the exact model calculation is 3.92%, because p=0.98 rather than exactly 1.
cards.text: Using 2q as a rare-recessive carrier estimate is an {{c1::approximation}} to 2pq.
cards.question: Using 2q as a rare-recessive carrier estimate is an {{c1::approximation}} to 2pq.

cards.explanation: These are broad demographic explanations, not a claim that all African populations share identical histories or diversity levels.
cards.text: The lecture links high African genetic diversity to a long population history and {{c1::out-of-Africa founder effects}}.
cards.question: The lecture links high African genetic diversity to a long population history and {{c1::out-of-Africa founder effects}}.

cards.explanation: The founder group may not carry all variants or the same frequencies as the source population.
cards.text: A new population founded by a small sample can show a {{c1::founder effect}}.
cards.question: A new population founded by a small sample can show a {{c1::founder effect}}.

cards.explanation: This is a demographic/drift effect, not evidence that founders were genetically superior or inferior.
cards.text: Founder events can reduce variation in descendants through {{c1::sampling of the source population}}.
cards.question: Founder events can reduce variation in descendants through {{c1::sampling of the source population}}.

cards.explanation: The slide connects population history with the size of correlated inherited segments; LD is a statistical association, not simply physical linkage.
cards.text: Non-random association of alleles at different loci is {{c1::linkage disequilibrium (LD)}}.
cards.question: Non-random association of alleles at different loci is {{c1::linkage disequilibrium (LD)}}.

cards.explanation: More recombination history can shorten shared haplotype blocks and reduce LD, while demography and selection also influence it.
cards.text: Over generations, recombination can break up associations between linked {{c1::alleles}}.
cards.question: Over generations, recombination can break up associations between linked {{c1::alleles}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture relates this to longer population history and lower average LD in many African populations. Lower LD and higher sequence diversity are related patterns, not identical measurements or a universal ranking of individuals.
cards.text: In the schematic, the African examples have {{c1::shorter shared haplotype blocks}}.
cards.question: In the schematic, the African examples have {{c1::shorter shared haplotype blocks}}.

cards.explanation: It is not a plot of disease burden, fitness or human worth. The selected dataset and population labels do not represent every individual in a continent.
cards.text: The diversity plot measures {{c1::variant sites per genome}} on its vertical axis.
cards.question: The diversity plot measures {{c1::variant sites per genome}} on its vertical axis.

cards.explanation: This is the illustrated population-level pattern, not a diagnostic rule assigning ancestry to an individual from one count.
cards.text: In the plotted dataset, the African-labelled samples generally have {{c1::more variant sites per genome}} than the European-labelled samples.
cards.question: In the plotted dataset, the African-labelled samples generally have {{c1::more variant sites per genome}} than the European-labelled samples.

cards.explanation: The slide’s “just a subset” diagram is a simplification: new mutations, later migration and archaic admixture mean it is not a literal claim that every non-African variant exists in every present-day African population.
cards.text: The out-of-Africa model explains why much non-African variation is {{c1::shared with African populations}}.
cards.question: The out-of-Africa model explains why much non-African variation is {{c1::shared with African populations}}.

cards.explanation: This does not deny genetic ancestry or population structure; those are measurable but do not map neatly onto fixed racial boxes.
cards.text: Social racial categories are not discrete biological {{c1::genetic partitions}} of humanity.
cards.question: Social racial categories are not discrete biological {{c1::genetic partitions}} of humanity.

cards.explanation: The lecture highlights ethnolinguistic groups as a sampling context. Such groups are not genetically uniform or closed, and identity does not determine an individual genotype.
cards.text: Language, geography and social mating patterns can influence population {{c1::genetic structure}}.
cards.question: Language, geography and social mating patterns can influence population {{c1::genetic structure}}.

cards.explanation: The figure names the loci and plots frequencies, but supplies no full variant identifiers or explanatory legend for every marker. No specific genotype, phenotype or selection coefficient is guessed.
cards.text: The KITLG, SLC24A5 and MC1R panels illustrate {{c1::different geographical allele-frequency patterns}}.
cards.question: The KITLG, SLC24A5 and MC1R panels illustrate {{c1::different geographical allele-frequency patterns}}.

cards.explanation: Non-random mating, population mixture, selection, sampling and genotyping problems can contribute. A close fit likewise does not prove all introductory assumptions hold.
cards.text: Departure from HWE proportions is a reason to {{c1::investigate further}} rather than a diagnosis of one evolutionary force.
cards.question: Departure from HWE proportions is a reason to {{c1::investigate further}} rather than a diagnosis of one evolutionary force.

slides.topic: Population Genetics II — Inheritance, Hardy–Weinberg & Diversity — page 2
slides.text:
L E A R N I N G  O B J E C T I V E S
By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:
• Demonstrate the use of a Punnett square to track the inheritance of 
alleles and genotypes
• Demonstrate the use of the Hardy-Weinberg law to calculate allele 
and genotype frequencies
• List the assumptions of the Hardy-Weinberg law
• List the forces that can change allele and genotype frequency
• Broadly explain global genetic diversity

slides.topic: Population Genetics II — Inheritance, Hardy–Weinberg & Diversity — page 3
slides.text:
R E V I E W
Studying normal 
variation
Normal genetic variation 
is a useful tool for 
understanding how 
humans differ from each 
other
Population genetics is 
the study of normal 
genetic variation and how 
it differs and changes 
over time

slides.topic: Population Genetics II — Inheritance, Hardy–Weinberg & Diversity — page 4
slides.text:
R E V I E W
Tracking variation
It is easiest to track variation in non-recombining portions of the human genome 
(the mitochondrial genome and on the Y chromosome)
However, this only provides information on matrilineal and patrilineal heritage
We need methods for understanding genetic variation across the genome

slides.topic: Population Genetics II — Inheritance, Hardy–Weinberg & Diversity — page 5
slides.text:
R E V I E W
PopGen lingo
When tracking 
genetic variation 
more broadly we 
concentrate on 
allelic, genotypic 
and phenotypic 
frequency

slides.topic: Population Genetics II — Inheritance, Hardy–Weinberg & Diversity — page 6
slides.text:
R E V I E W
Shuffling
Inheritance: the process whereby individuals 
inherit and transmit to their offspring one 
out of the two alleles present in 
homologous chromosomes. 
The first person to formally study 
inheritance was Gregor Mendel, who 
proposed several laws of inheritance
Gregor Mendel
(1822-1884)

slides.topic: Population Genetics II — Inheritance, Hardy–Weinberg & Diversity — page 7
slides.text:
M E N D E L ’ S  L A W S
The Law of Segregation
Individuals possess two alleles for each trait, and these alleles 
segregate during meiosis, such that each parent passes only one allele 
to their offspring
The Law of Independent Assortment
The inheritance of one pair of alleles is independent of the other pair
The Law of Dominance
The expression of recessive alleles will always be masked by dominant 
alleles

slides.topic: Population Genetics II — Inheritance, Hardy–Weinberg & Diversity — page 14
slides.text:
P O P U L A T I O N S
Expanding the scope
We know how to follow inheritance when considering two individuals at a time, which is sufficient to track genotype 
and allele frequencies when studying a small population of organisms while focussing on just a few traits. 
But how can we can track genotype and allele frequencies across larger populations, over many generations?

slides.topic: Population Genetics II — Inheritance, Hardy–Weinberg & Diversity — page 15
slides.text:
P O P U L A T I O N S
Red hair
Red hair is recessive to all other hair colours. To express red hair, an individual must be homozygous for the red hair 
allele, which only occurs in about 2% of the general population.
What do you think will happen to the general prevalence of red hair? Will it increase, decrease, or stay the same over 
time?

slides.topic: Population Genetics II — Inheritance, Hardy–Weinberg & Diversity — page 16
slides.text:
H A R D Y - W E I N B E R G  L A W
Solving the riddle
The answer to this question was discovered using basic mathematical modelling, by two 
independent scientists: D.H. Hardy and Wilhelm Weinberg
Imagine a population of individuals with a gene 
comprising two alleles, A and a. Assume the A allele has 
a frequency of 70% while the a allele has a frequency 
of 30%
A + a = 0.7 + 0.3 = 1  (all possible alleles)
The chance of observing an AA individual:
AA = 0.7 x 0.7 = 0.49
aa = 0.3 x 0.3 = 0.09
Aa = 0.7 x 0.3 = 0.21
aA = 0.3 x 0.7 = 0.21
0.49 + 2(0.21) + 0.09 = 1 (all possible genotypes)

slides.topic: Population Genetics II — Inheritance, Hardy–Weinberg & Diversity — page 17
slides.text:
H A R D Y - W E I N B E R G  L A W
Back to Punnet squares
What will happen to the allele and genotype 
frequencies in the next generation of offspring? 
What is any child’s chance of receiving an A 
allele?
0.49 + 0.5(0.42) = 0.7
What is any child’s chance of receiving an a 
allele?
0.5(0.42) + 0.09 = 0.3
The allele frequency has not changed in the 
next generation!

by using algebraic notation:
Let the frequency of allele 1 = p
Let the frequency of allele 2 = q
p + q = 1
p2 + 2pq + q2 = 1
This is known as the Hardy-
Weinberg law

slides.topic: Population Genetics II — Inheritance, Hardy–Weinberg & Diversity — page 19
slides.text:
H A R D Y - W E I N B E R G  E Q U I L I B R I U M
Variation is maintained
The Hardy-Weinberg law suggests genotypic and allele frequencies remain 
constant each generation
That is, they are in a state of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
This conclusion is confusing, because we know there are forces and events that 
DO change allele and genotype frequencies over time:
1. Mating pattern
2. Migration
3. Mutation and recombination
4. Selection
5. Bottlenecks
6. Genetic drift

slides.topic: Population Genetics II — Inheritance, Hardy–Weinberg & Diversity — page 26
slides.text:
A S S U M P T I O N S
Clarifying the confusion
If there are so many forces that can alter allele and 
genotype frequency, how can the HW law conclude 
that frequencies don’t change??
The Hardy-Weinberg law makes many assumptions:
1. The organism is diploid
2. Reproduction is sexual 
3. Generations are non-overlapping
4. The gene under consideration has two alleles
5.  Allele frequencies are identical in females and males

slides.topic: Population Genetics II — Inheritance, Hardy–Weinberg & Diversity — page 27
slides.text:
A S S U M P T I O N S
6. Individuals of all genotypes 
have equal rates of survival and 
equal reproductive success i.e. 
no selection
7. No mutation
8. No migration
9. Infinitely large population
10. Individuals mate randomly

U T I L I T Y  O F  H W  L A W
If humans violate most of the assumptions of the Hardy-Weinberg law,

p = 0.89; p2 = 0.792
q = 0.11; q2 = 0.012
2pq = 0.1958
Observed = 0.79; 0.20; 0.01
These alleles are in Hardy-Weinberg 
equilibrium!

Is it a race?
Race is a social construct. Racial 
categories are not supported by genetic 
evidence
People of the same ethnicity, that speak 
the same language, tend to interbreed
Population genetics is concerned with 
comparing allele/genotype/phenotype 
ratios across ethnolinguistic groups, not

slides.topic: Population Genetics II — Inheritance, Hardy–Weinberg & Diversity — page 43
slides.text:
S U M M A R Y
Tracking genetic variation across populations and over time requires 
calculation of allelic, genotypic, and phenotypic frequencies
This calculation can be done using the Hardy-Weinberg law. In general, the 
law confirms that genetic variability is maintained over time and most 
alleles/genotypes in a population are in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
Alleles/genotypes not in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium are likely being 
affected by real-world forces
People of the same ethnic and language groups tend to stick together, 
meaning that allele and genotype frequences differ by ethnolinguistic 
groups
